title: Practice CFA Fundamentals with RecallForge
thumbnailHeadline:
CFA fundamentals
From answer to understanding.

scenes.title: Start with the fundamentals
scenes.narration: This demonstration is for learners reviewing introductory investment concepts. Recall Forge is a practice workspace, not an official course or a substitute for your examination curriculum. Choose the C F A fundamentals demo from the sample chooser. It contains ten original questions, explanations, and public reference links.

scenes.title: Read the assumptions
scenes.narration: Start with the compounding question. Ten thousand earns five percent per year for two years. There are no deposits, withdrawals, fees, or taxes in this stated example. Reading those assumptions matters, because a change in cash flows or compounding frequency would change the calculation. Work out the answer before checking it.

scenes.title: Compound both years
scenes.narration: Five percent growth means multiplying by one point zero five for each year. After the first year, the value is ten thousand five hundred. The second year earns interest on that larger balance. The result is eleven thousand and twenty-five. Select that answer and use Check answer to inspect the reasoning and reference.

scenes.title: Learn from an error
scenes.narration: Now consider present value. A payment of twelve hundred and ten arrives in two years, discounted at ten percent annually. We deliberately selected eleven hundred to show the mistake workflow. That discounts only one year. Dividing by one point one twice gives one thousand today. The explanation helps locate the missing step.

scenes.title: Interpret the result honestly
scenes.narration: Submitting creates an answer review and topic breakdown. In this recorded demonstration, only two questions were answered and the others were skipped. The displayed score reflects that incomplete session. It is not a claim about exam performance. Review the individual reasoning rather than drawing conclusions from a tiny or intentionally incomplete sample.

scenes.title: Retest what needs work
scenes.narration: Retest wrong answers creates a study session from wrong and skipped questions. Correct questions from the original attempt are excluded. The order may change because the retest shuffles its questions. This lets you focus your next pass on unresolved concepts, then check whether the reasoning now makes sense rather than merely remembering an option letter.

scenes.title: Build a repeatable routine
scenes.narration: Daily revision gives saved questions another turn over time. Confident correct reviews can advance through the schedule; guesses and mistakes return sooner. Use the library to revisit the complete pack whenever needed. The other questions introduce returns, diversification, allocation, rebalancing, bond interest-rate risk, costs, and the investment time horizon.

scenes.title: Keep context with progress
scenes.narration: Progress retains attempt details and topic signals. The example records here belong only to the disposable demonstration workspace. Mixed packs are not directly comparable, and a few questions do not establish mastery. Pair these signals with your own study plan and reliable reference material. Export a backup before moving to another browser or device.

title: Practice FRM Risk Concepts with RecallForge
thumbnailHeadline:
FRM risk concepts
Make the assumptions explicit.

scenes.title: A focused risk demo
scenes.narration: This walkthrough introduces financial risk concepts using Recall Forge. Choose the F R M risk concepts demo to try ten original questions. They cover simplified credit loss, probabilities, risk categories, concentration, and model assumptions. These are introductory learning examples, not official exam questions, regulatory capital calculations, or a complete preparation course.

scenes.title: Separate the risk inputs
scenes.narration: The first example states a two percent default probability, forty percent loss given default, and an exposure of one hundred thousand. Each input has a different meaning. Probability describes how likely default is in the model. Loss given default describes the fraction lost if default occurs. Exposure describes the amount at risk when it happens.

scenes.title: Do not confuse severity with average
scenes.narration: We deliberately chose forty thousand to demonstrate a common conceptual mix-up. That is the loss conditional on default in this simplified example. Expected loss also weights that amount by the two percent default probability. Multiply zero point zero two by zero point four by one hundred thousand. The resulting expected loss is eight hundred.

scenes.title: Check the reasoning and source
scenes.narration: Check answer shows the multiplication and links to the reference. Expected loss is an average under the stated model. It is not the largest possible loss, and it does not guarantee what will happen to an individual exposure. Treat the explanation as a reason to inspect your assumptions, not as a replacement for understanding the underlying risk.

scenes.title: Connect recovery and loss
scenes.narration: The next example asks what remains after recovering sixty percent of exposure. With no extra costs in the stated model, forty percent remains unrecovered. That is the simplified loss-given-default fraction. Different costs, collateral assumptions, or recovery timing could require a richer calculation. This introductory question makes the simplification explicit before asking for the answer.

scenes.title: Use the review to plan another pass
scenes.narration: The displayed result comes from a deliberately incomplete demonstration with a wrong answer and skipped questions. It separates correct, wrong, and skipped outcomes. Review the explanation for the mistake, then retest unresolved questions. A low demo score is not evidence about your ability, and a high score on ten questions would not establish examination readiness either.

scenes.title: Broaden the concepts
scenes.narration: The remaining questions distinguish credit, liquidity, and operational risk, and explain why a single industry can leave concentration exposure. Probability examples require stated outcomes and weights. Normal-model examples require the normal assumption. The pack also introduces why expected shortfall describes tail severity. Each question includes a public reference rather than copied examination-provider material.

scenes.title: Keep the revision loop local
scenes.narration: After studying, use Daily revision to revisit saved questions. Mark your confidence honestly, especially when an answer was a guess. Correct guesses do not mean a concept is secure. Your study records remain local to this browser and site address. Download a portable backup in Settings before changing devices or clearing the browser’s stored data.

title: Practice CMT Technical Analysis with RecallForge
thumbnailHeadline:
CMT technical analysis
Understand the indicator.

scenes.title: Start with chart concepts
scenes.narration: Choose the C M T technical analysis demo in Recall Forge. It contains ten original introductory questions about moving averages, trend structure, support and resistance, momentum, and indicator limitations. This is independent practice, not official examination content or a trading recommendation. The goal is to understand a concept and its limits before moving to another question.

scenes.title: Calculate a simple average
scenes.narration: The first question gives closing prices of ten, twelve, and fourteen. A three-period simple moving average uses all three closes with equal weights. Add the values to get thirty-six, then divide by three. The answer is twelve. Work the calculation yourself before selecting an option, so feedback tests your reasoning rather than only your recognition.

scenes.title: Understand the rolling window
scenes.narration: Check answer shows how the average was calculated and links to the source. If the next closing price is sixteen, the latest three-period window becomes twelve, fourteen, and sixteen. Ten drops out of the calculation. The updated average is fourteen. A moving window uses the latest observations, not every value that has appeared since the beginning.

scenes.title: Watch the smoothing tradeoff
scenes.narration: A longer moving average generally smooths more short-term variation and reacts more slowly to recent changes. An exponential moving average instead gives more weight to recent prices. Neither approach eliminates uncertainty. Indicators describe and summarize price behavior; they do not guarantee the next move. The demo asks about those distinctions rather than promising a profitable signal.

scenes.title: Interpret momentum in context
scenes.narration: Under the traditional seventy and thirty convention, a relative strength index reading of seventy-five is described as overbought. Choose that description, then inspect the explanation. Overbought does not mean the next bar must decline. A strong trend can keep an oscillator near an extreme for a considerable time, so context remains part of the interpretation.

scenes.title: Keep the limitation beside the label
scenes.narration: The feedback states both the conventional label and its limitation. The next question asks why an oscillator can remain overbought during an upward trend. Support and resistance questions make a similar distinction: observed buying or selling areas can affect price behavior, but they are not permanent barriers that prices can never cross. Read the explanation rather than memorizing an absolute rule.

scenes.title: Review concepts instead of option letters
scenes.narration: The same Recall Forge workflow supports targeted retesting across all packs. After submission, wrong and skipped questions can return in a new study session. This screen illustrates the shared retest feature using the investment pack. Keep attention on the concept, because question order or option order can change when shuffling is enabled.

scenes.title: Return with a study routine
scenes.narration: Daily revision brings saved concepts back for another look. Confidence ratings help distinguish an understood answer from a guess. Progress stores detailed attempts, but a small sample cannot establish mastery. These screens contain disposable demonstration records. Your own local workspace will contain your attempts, and a portable backup lets you preserve them when moving between devices.
